LHCb has conducted a detailed study of the decay of $B^0_s$ mesons into two identical $K^+K^-$ mesons, based on nearly the entire data set from LHC Run 1 and Run 2. Through an intricate analysis of the decay time distribution, researchers have determined a key parameter, x, with high precision. This parameter plays a crucial role in a fundamental equation that describes the difference in the number of $B^0_s$ and $ \bar{B^0_s}$ mesons. By combining several experimental and theoretical inputs, the study provides the most precise measurement of this meson-antimeson mixing parameter to date, namely, $-0.56 \pm 0.14 \pm 0.11 \pm 0.13 \pm 0.03(i)$.  Additionally, the study predicts a similar outcome for a related but as-of-yet unmeasured decay, $ \bar{B^0_s}\rightarrow K^+K^-$, with an even smaller confidence interval, namely, $-0.51 \pm 0.09 \pm 0.08 \pm 0.13 \pm 0.03(i)$.

This research paper focuses on the discrete approximation of a control system governed by a stochastic partial differential equation with a distributed control, aimed at achieving a tolerance level within a specified time frame. The system's behavior is modeled by a parabolic stochastic equation with the control term contributing to the regularization effect. Both existence and convergence rates of discretized solutions, particularly with implicit- Euler or backward differentiation formulas, are examined in a discrete setting.

The highest-energy particles reaching Earth from space primarily originate from beyond our galaxy. A new investigation into these extragalactic cosmic rays above 4.06 EeV demonstrates a strong pattern of directionality when observed from the Southern Hemisphere. This finding contradicts the assumption that these very high-energy particles behave as if they were randomly scattered. Instead, data indicates that at this energy level, a substantial portion of the cosmic-ray population maintains clear links to their source, likely formed by normal matter within our universe.

This study presents analyses of p+Pb interactions at a center-of-energy interval of 5.02 TeV, utilizing the ATLAS detector. Data were collected and categorized by rapidity intervals from -4.47 to -2.58 and 2.58 to 4.47 in addition to centrality. The research involved in-depth examination of charge symmetry, neutrality, and particle supression properties, specifically related to p+Pb interactions. Detailed examination of the spatial distribution of particles was conducted through analysis of the ATLAS detector's charged particle mobility. Furthermore, studies on nuclear modification factors were conducted based on the transverse momentum of particles and the orientation of the event plane, revealing influence of the nuclear structure on particle production dynamics.

In this report, we examine quantum mechanical systems described by a noncommutative torus, utilizing a specific set of operator representations. Our analysis indicates that, for any given Lie algebra, we can directly compute its discrete spectrum and corresponding eigenfunctions. Additionally, we have meaningful expressions for the discrete spectrum of several systems, such as the isotonic oscillator, the SU(1,1) oscillator, and the noncommutative isotonic oscillator, as well as some asymptotic formulas. Furthermore, our operator framework yields trivial proof of the Rayleigh-Quotient inequality.

A precise estimation of categorizing the five types of tumor cells, specifically identifying small, large, immunoblastic, intermediate, and plasma cells, is crucial for enhancing the reliability of federated learning models trained on segmented and classified whole-slide images. This study explores the challenges of federated classification when confronted with such a complex labeling task. Furthermore, an application to real-world data is presented, demonstrating the performance of federated models as local datasets become more substantial. This research is centered around a model designed to categorize TILs within whole-slide images of breast cancer patients, an environment that naturally embodies a federated setting and possesses complete image labels. This unified framework facilitates comparisons between models trained using image classification, multi-model training with independent data splits, and federated learning techniques.

Equalization techniques are used to improve a optical line terminal's signal-to-noise ratio in long-distance, underwater communication systems. However, a decision feedback equalizer, which is an effective method for compensating for chromatic dispersion in this type of system, suffers from a issue where large intensity modulations cause symbol errors to be transferred to adjacent symbols on a submarine cable. This problem is particularly severe in areas of the underwater link with high dispersion values. We developed a method to mitigate this error propagation, which identifies and eliminates feedback from affected symbols on a marine link with multiple pressure zones. We implemented our solution on a underwater communication link with multiple pressure zones and observed a significant decrease in bit error rate performance loss associated with this error mitigation. Our research is published in the Journal of Lightwave Technology in 2023.

Deep learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) have gained significant popularity in time-series analysis and achieved superior performance. However, their considerable computational demands hindered their deployment in real-world applications. While recent studies attempted to reduce TCNs' complexity through knowledge distillation or network optimization, they often resulted in substantial increases in network complexity, particularly when employing parallel network structures. In response, we propose a novel optimizer called Pruning In Time (PIT) that effectively reduces TCN complexity without compromising performance. PIT's innovative mechanism selectively removes unnecessary filters and activations across time, yielding an efficient and lightweight model. The PIT-optimized TCN models maintain a straightforward network structure, facilitating efficient training and inference. Our experiments reveal that PIT outperforms existing methods in both model accuracy and efficiency, exhibiting better F1-scores and fewer floating-point operations (MFALOPs) across various time-series datasets and TCN backbones. Notably, the PIT-optimized TCN models excel in fault detection and diagnosis, outperforming existing optimization approaches in both accuracy and efficiency.

The lower central series of a free zinbiel algebra of characteristic not equal to 2 has been found to be derived series equivalent, with the distinction being that in characteristic 2, it is two steps slower.

Our analysis aims to deepen the investigation of fluctuations in charged-particle flow components along both plane A and B at the LHC, with focus on Pb-Pb collisions at a high energy of 5.02 TeV. We assess the sensitivity of $v_n\{4\}$ fluctuation measurements to one-dimensional flow angle variations, finding a significant impact from these fluctuations on fourth-order fluctuations. In contrast, sensitivity to minor sensitivities to minor variations in magnitudes of these flows is found. The observed data exhibits lower fluctuations than expected, with this discrepancy particularly pronounced for fourth-order fluctuations. Additionally, we find the impact of these fluctuations on mixed correlations of the form $\langle v_2\,v_3\rangle_{\rm MP}$ to be negligible.

The concept of differential linear equations was first explored by S. L. Lee in 2003, and the DLE-Logics framework for this type of equation has since been developed by various researchers. This development has included both a forward inference system, initially proposed by S. L. Lee and later expanded, as well as an inverse system. The existing unified representations for both single and multiple differential linear equations have primarily focused on the DLE-Logics framework for equations with the same differential order. This research has now introduced a set of operators and rules for handling differential linear equations of varying orders, and proven that this system is complete, ultimately showing that it can be viewed as an extension of the existing DLE-Logics framework.

The study examines a well-established set of rules for characterizing inconsistencies in data tables, specifically focusing on null values and a generalization of dependency patterns used to describe data relationships. The researchers then set out to create strategies for removing inconsistencies from these data tables, targeting scenarios where one relationship implies another, and implemenen these solutions for both specific cases and a broader, abstract framework. Furthermore, this work serves as a foundation for developing techniques to resolve conflicts in data tables, whether involving null values, relationships, or both, within the domain of data cleaning.

This research develops a novel statistical model known as time-dependent Poisson autoregression, which offers an enhanced understanding of dynamic processes modeled by GARMA models. A specific implementation, the TPIP, is introduced based on this concept. Estimation is achieved through maximum likelihood estimation, utilizing a efficient approach involving integral approximation and the Newton-Raphson method. Key properties of the estimator are established both theoretically for stationary processes and simulation-wise in non-stationary contexts. A limited set of existing models, including constant and matricial exponents in Bayesian dynamic linear models, serves as point of comparison. A range of artificial data sets, along with real-world examples from energy consumption, inflation rates, and COVID infections, guides the discussion on the model's applicability.

When developing autonomous systems, robotics projects and autonomous driving, creating digital models of objects in the environment is a crucial step. This step involves representing objects in scenes to facilitate tasks like navigation, interaction and NLP. Current object models based on point clouds are extensive but fall short in covering all aspects of object interaction, NLP and NLO. They also struggle with object recognition in low-point-cloud-density scenarios, which are inevitable in robotic and autonomous applications. To overcome these challenges, we propose Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel representation that encodes object properties over a coarse spatial grid, efficiently capturing object information regardless of point cloud data. NDFs are compatible with both point clouds and images, allowing for robust object interaction, NLP and navigation. To handle objects efficiently in 3D space, we employ rotationally-symmetric descriptors, reducing the representation's dimensionality and ensuring consistency across angles. To process these NDFs, we develop tasks-specific Neural Networks, demonstrating our approach's effectiveness in object detection, contact prediction, stable object manipulation, and natural and natural-language-guided navigation.

The SiD Detector is one of the two streamlined designs proposed for the future linear linear collider, specifically designed to minimize background particles reaching the detection device for outstanding accuracy. To enhance the SiD Detector's capabilities, particularly in lepton direction identification and hadron reconstruction, a new SiD prototype is being constructed by a collaborative group. This new design features improved rotation sensors using SiD's design principles but with SiD Detector's specific characteristics. By building and testing these new rotation sensors, the collaboration aims to gather valuable data on assembly, functional testing, and integration during the SiD's construction phase. Additionally, this project serves as an educational platform for early-career researchers in the field.

Researchers examined the reddening map of Tonantzintla 2, a dense star cluster in the Galactic bulge, to investigate its physical characteristics. By analyzing the cluster's spectrum, they discovered evidence of distinct subpopulations in several wavelength ranges, including the visible, infrared, and UV regions. However, the degree of separation between these populations varied across the ranges. They determined that the cluster's rotation speed is approximately 140 km/s, with a relatively narrow distribution. Additionally, they found that the cluster's mass density is heavily concentrated towards its center, following a cubic power law. They estimated a spherical mass of around $4.2 \times 10^8 \, \textrm{kg}$, about 1.5 times the flat rotation curve regime. The mass decensity regime extends for several hundred parsecs, potentially contributing to the bulge's overall mass. They also discovered evidence of a massive stream, with a mass exceeding $10^8 \, \sun$, extending from the cluster to an elongated region. Exploring this region may reveal a larger portion of the cluster's mass.

The growth of library-based formalization has significantly contributed to the expansion of the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs over the past decade. As a consequence, the task of proving new theorems has become increasingly complex due to the vast number of dependent definitions incorporated. To address this issue of compositionality, we have developed a framework to assess and enhance large Isabelle theories by examining and modifying their definitions through the analysis of proof term generation. Specifically, we propose a set of criteria to evaluate the impact of defining new constants on the proofs of existing propositions, categorize theories based on their compositional nature, and outline strategies for enhancing non-compositional theories. Furthermore, we have developed a method to anticipate the effect of defining new constants on existing proof terms, as well as to examine the consequences of extending definitions on existing proof term reachability. To illustrate our approach, we have applied it to the Isabelle theories related to Verifiable Machine Learning, resulting in substantial improvements to the verbosity of mixed-integer programming encodings by nearly an order of magnitude.

Recently, universal characteristics of the grand canonical quantum Heisenberg model have been investigated through the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity in the magnetic field strength. A study drawn from prior research has applied the same analysis to the classic Heisenberg model and has been extended to encompass O(N) models, encompassing both Heisenberg (O(3)) and ferromagnetic Ising (O(2)) cases. By employing Monte Carlo simulations, researchers have determined the critical exponent $\vartheta$ and precise location of the phase transition point $h/v$ for multiple values of $N$, and found that in the thermodynamic limit, this position is determined solely by the ratio of these parameters, and is universal in nature. Notably, a newly discovered theory posits that the Yang-Lee edge singularity is linked to an isolated critical point within the Ising universality class, and surprising evidence suggests that this is valid for all classic O(N) models. Furthermore, a novel, theoretically founded methodology circumventing the limitations imposed by finite-size effects in Monte Carlo simulations enables direct measurement of $\vartheta$ and (h/v) for all values of $N\ge2$, and with only two fit parameters, yields highly precise results of $ \vartheta = 5/16\, $ and $ \text{h/v} = 1.03082(6)\, $ for Heisenberg, and $ \vartheta = 2

In statistics and machine learning, the "larger is better" principle states that expected values increase when adding non-negative random variables under any given condition. We establish a corresponding principle for neural networks called the "free energy of better" which states the expected optimization landscape's local minima decrease significantly as more data is incorporated, under certain conditions. We derive this principle formally and then apply it to neural networks by demonstrating that, under a specific prior, the TAP free energy landscape's local minima and its associated probability distribution at zero temperature both worsen when increasing network network width. We provide an explicit calculation showing the expected Sudakov-Fernique principle can be extracted from the TAP free energy free energy landscape and demonstrate that under certain network conditions it implies the TAP free energy landscape is concave.

Two novel methods have been introduced for modeling anisotropic metasurfaces within the frequency domain, which can model extremely high rotational symmetries efficiently. By testing various configurations with up to 108-fold symmetry, it was demonstrated that these methods yield highly accurate results with minimal computational resources, providing results within 0.5 percent of direct simulations using fewer than 10 thousand time-domain elements. Furthermore, one method has proven particularly effective for multilayer structures, resulting in less than 1 percent deviation from direct simulations with approximately 30 percent of the computational elements. These methods have been utilized to examine the properties of metasurfaces designed for polarisation conversion and frequency selection, as well as multilayer architectures for waveband separation, whereas traditional modeling techniques are limited to lower symmetries due to their reliance on 2D adaptations of 3D simulations.

The primary objective of this research is to validate the smooth local orbital linearization theorem for smooth vector fields with a full set of first integrals near non-degenerate equilibrium points. Additionally, we will validate the local orbital linearization theorem for smooth quotient vector fields resulting from such systems, under specific technical conditions.

The substantial dimensionality of the configuration interaction space for multi-electron systems presents a significant challenge, which can potentially be addressed by applying deep neural networks to solve the electronic Schrödinger equation directly. In this research, a novel configuration interaction estimator is proposed, demonstrating enhanced stability and higher accuracy compared to existing methods. Notably, this approach is successfully applied to a range of benchmark tests, including homogeneous electron gas, hydrogen molecule, beryllium atom, and carbon dioxide molecule, where it accurately predicts complete configuration correlation limitations in a range of interatomic distances and molecular orientations.

This paper discusses three distinct galactic structures identified in a deep, wide-field infrared survey of the Coma cluster of galaxies. Firstly, we catalogue nearly 6000 spiral galaxies in the cluster's central regions, dubbed the Combarica, characterized by high density and diverse inclination. Secondly, we discover nearly 3000 early-type galaxies forming a semi-circular pattern in the cluster's southern half, named the Coma elliptical Semi-circle. These galaxies exhibit elevated specific stellar formation rates, often exceeding their surrounding environments. Moreover, there's a distinct alignment along the same plane and magnetic field as the Combarica. Lastly, we identify a massive elliptical galaxy chain spanning the southern half-sky of the cluster, consisting of nearly 400 massive elliptical galaxies, each with stellar formation rates in the top 10%, exceeding their neighboring densities by nearly 50%. These structures, the Combarica, the Coma elliptical Semi-circle, and the massive elliptical chain, reveal significant spatial and stellar formation pattern similarities, suggesting a potential influence of the large-scale cosmic web on semi-circular great circles, great arcs, and significant intersections. These formations may have formed due to the merging of filaments in the cosmic web that shaped the half-sky of the Coma cluster.

While modern cities' air quality monitoring is primarily done with dedicated measurement devices, using photometric data from visible stars as an alternative is being more closely examined. By analyzing the color changes in stars caused as their light traverses the atmosphere, this method can be used to monitor local air quality and map urban pollution. A data set comparing traditional aerosol measurements with those derived from nightly stellar photometry demonstrates the potential of this approach for several urban areas, on a continuous basis.

Recently, estimating a object's 6D pose using deep learning has gained significant attention due to its importance in downstream tasks like deep surgery planning and quality inspection of manufactured goods. While most existing methods focus on predicting two-dimensional pose by ignoring the depth dimension, this approach often leads to ambiguities in pose estimation. Conversely, directly estimating 6D pose although possible, typically yields suboptimal results due to the difficulty of designing comprehensive training samples that cover all 6D pose combinations. To overcome this issue, we propose a novel two-stage framework for 6D pose prediction, initially employing clustering and projection techniques to resolve pose ambiguities, and subsequently utilizing deep learning to estimate 2D pose. Our initial step involves projecting 3D pose-combinatorial samples onto a 2D plane and applying K-means to generate discrete pose hypotheses. To effectively resolve pose ambiguities in regions of interest, we then compute a Deep Orientation Score Map by scoring each hypothesis. Only the most highly scored hypotheses are considered, and in our final step, we train a DeepHighlyAmbiguousProjectionHMap (DeepHMap) to estimate 2D pose. For efficiency, we introduce a regression step to predict the selected hypotheses. Our method achieves state-of-the-art 6D pose prediction accuracy, surpassing current state-of-the-art methods by 12% on a challenging benchmark dataset.

Peridynamic theories have seen a significant expansion in the last decade, with research efforts focused on developing nonlocal models of fluids and solids. This paper explores bond-based peridynamics in detail and addresses key challenges associated with bond-based dynamic stress points. It also delves into recent breakthroughs in this field, particularly the development of generalized bond-based models capable of capturing rupture-induced stress point failure. Additionally, this research presents an innovative variant of the moving least-square method that ensures stability and convergence, simultaneously preserving the first integral of motion during simulations. The findings presented here lay the groundwork for a broader investigation into peridynamic fluid models and their underlying principles.

We are introducing a Python library called GGLasso that facilitates the
execution of the Universal Graphical Lasso algorithm as described by
Kooijman, Giordano, and Lise (2019). This particular algorithm is effective
for handling large-scale, densely structured datasets. By utilizing GGLasso,
researchers can easily perform tasks such as hypothesis testing, Hirschfeld-Gebelein-Renyi
maximal correlation computation, and post-selection inference on the obtained
graph estimates.

Designing drug candidates that target proteins' active sites is a crucial step in the pharmaceutical development process. Many proteins, however, have complex shapes with multiple active sites in various parts of their structure, posing a challenge for molecular modeling methods used in drug design. This study presents a novel molecular dynamics approach called cLiTLE that can efficiently configure large and intricate proteins by sampling their conformational space. The cLiTLE method drives the protein's folds into stable configurations at the target temperature and provides an effective "glue" to bring distinct domains together, even in proteins with five or more domains. Additionally, this method was applied to the case of anti-sense drug target, human apolipoprotein E, and demonstrated its capability to identify multiple disjoint active sites through configuration optimization.

We've investigated how the presence of dark matter with long-range forces, which create wave-like patterns, may affect the gravitational waves produced by merging supermassive black holes with varying properties. Our team utilized numerical relativity to generate three-dimensional simulations that capture the interaction of multiple gravitational potential waves with the black holes, in accordance with post-Newtonian predictions before they collide. From these simulations, we derived orbital parameters and final masses/spins of the resulting black holes, which we then analyzed in depth. In particular, we observed that the gravitational waves caused the black holes to move in orbital paths that gradually decayed due to friction, in some cases producing detectable saw-tooth patterns in the gravitational waves produced. We believe these features could one day be identified by future gravitational wave detectors that have high sensitivity.

Consider an extended Euler-Bernoulli beam consisting of $N$ segments connected at an vertex, we establish the uniform $p$-stability of its dynamics when each segment rests on a different Kelvin-Voigt foundation and is connected to $p$ distinct edges with dampers, where $p$ is greater than or equal to two. Notably, our proof reveals that certain symmetry must be maintained among the foundation coefficients and the damper values. However, through application of the Lagrange method and utilizing the properties of the resulting OMPDEs with characteristic values, we demonstrate that strict symmetry requirements are not solely decisive in determining stability.

Traditional photoacoustic tomography systems rely on direct detection, where sensors measure acoustic signals directly, but this method's spatial resolution is limited by the size of the sensors. An alternative approach involves placing sensors behind a sonic lens that focuses acoustic waves, allowing for the use of smaller sensors and potentially improving spatial resolution, but the effectiveness of this method has not been thoroughly examined due to inconsistencies in prior experimental setups. In this study, several sonic lens materials were evaluated using consistent measurements, and it was demonstrated that combining a high-impedance lens cap with a lower-impedance polymer sonodeformable layer minimizes mismatches and provides optimal focusing, even for ultrasound frequencies as high as 2.25 MHz. Experimental results showed excellent focus at 1 MHz and the systems' response was nearly linear within 150 kPa. These findings provide the first consistent evidence for the viability of sonic lenses in photoacoustic tomography, with significant implications for future sensor design and system configuration.

The concept of node reliance in the network community has been explored, with a significant finding that nodes within the same community often demonstrate mutual reliance on one another. A novel metric of node reliance within multi-layered networks has been devised, accounting for both intra and inter-layer connections, and the corresponding eigenvector dependence centrality was derived. Theoretical analysis proves that the centroid of the reliance eigenvector corresponds to the maximum of the objective function. The proposed method was evaluated using synthetic and real-world multi-layer networks, with results indicating that it effectively identifies nodes with high reliance and clusters nodes into communities with comparable reliance patterns. Additionally, it outperformed existing methods of node classification in real-world multi-layer networks.

We tackle the issue of removing noise and mosaics from images that have been blurred, using a novel deep learning approach called D^3. This model uniquely combines all four processes and learns to handle them simultaneously in a single step. By training on pairs of training images with controlled noise levels and blur effects, D^3 can infer the underlying sharp image without needing to know the specific kernel or noise pattern. We evaluate its performance on single-shot spectral imaging and low-light photography, and also explore its use in real-time low-light demosaicking. Our results show that D^3 achieves the highest quality images in all scenarios, and we optimize it for real-time processing.

Recently, we derived the Dirac equation within the noncommutative framework of $R$-Minkowski space-time, utilizing the Hadamard operator. In this study, we perform a series of expansions based on the parameter $\hat{x}_{\mu}$ to obtain approximately commutative forms for various types of fields, including scalar, gauge, and spinor fields. Subsequently, we apply these expansions to the commutator structure functions of the Hadamard algebra, yielding new, nontrivial instances.

This paper introduces the Causal Exploration Toolbox (CAT), a set of methods
for analyzing causal connections and presenting visual representations.
Designed as an iterative framework for stepwise model development, CAT
incorporates effect size metrics, along with scatter plot matrices and directed
graphs to effectively communicate complex information. Additionally, CAT is
customizable for the purpose of integrating various strategies, such as
linear regression, in the pursuit of uncovering general patterns.

This study investigates how spheres with varying depths of submersion and velocities impact a water surface, and analyzes the formation of an air-water seal upon impact. Specifically, we focus on spheres made of rubber that are dropped into water and observe the factors influencing the seal. Both theoretical calculations and high-speed video recordings are used to examine air escape patterns and other phenomena. Our research identifies a new, broader range of velocities where an air pocket forms, filling the gap between low and relatively fast impact speed regimes.

A 2-form gauge field is studied within a class of Type IIB vacua characterized by specific background fields and fluxes, comprising the dilaxion field, O6-planes, and (3,0) flux. Through an analysis of these components under various breakings of the Type IIB supergravity theory's U(1)_A symmetry, we determine the nature and effects of each term in the resulting four-dimensional effective field theory Lagrangian. Notably, the interaction between the 2-form field and axionic descent descendants of the anomaly associated with U(1)_A symmetry breaking gives rise to two distinct global symmetry-protecting theta-terms that diverge from previously identified theta-terms in such models. From the theoretical framework of the bulk 2-form field, we derive the value of the global symmetry-protected theta angle. Additionally, by considering massive IIB supergravity with its tower of Kaluza-Klein modes, we establish the validity of this setup and its associated theta angle value within the broader context of consistent higher-derivative corrections.

Mobile devices frequently run multiple security-sensitive applications concurrently, necessitating isolation mechanisms to prevent data breaches.  A common approach involves allocating distinct physical hardware resources to each app, which is reliable but comes with a drawback: wasted hardware due to unused memory.  This inefficiency becomes apparent as applications utilize varying amounts of memory during operation.  We investigate a question arising from this challenge--whether we can achieve the minimum trust requirement of zero-interference apps while also maximizing hardware utility.  In essence, we seek a device with smaller hardware specifications that can efficiently host in-use applications within isolated environments.  As it turns out, this challenge is theoretically insoluble; nonetheless, we identify only those apps for which solutions exist, characterized by a partial order relationship.  This discovery significantly informs device designers about the class of apps suitable for hardware optimization.  We validate this finding with a practical implementation, demonstrating a 25% reduction in necessary hardware for paired apps within this category.  This research provides crucial theoretical and empirical insights into hardware isolation efficiency, potentially advancing mobile device hardware design.

We are concerned with the robust optimization of policies in reinforcement learning systems that are subject to severe malfunctions, such as those caused by sophisticated adversarial influences. Our goal is to develop a robust policy optimization algorithm capable of withstanding such corruptions. Traditional robust optimization approaches, formulated as min-max problems, prove to be ineffective due to their sensitivity and high computational demands. Instead, we reformulate the problem into a more tractable form and propose an innovative robust policy gradient method, which minimizes a potentially distorted loss function in a gradient-compliant manner. Our experiments on distinct environments, consisting of synthetic datasets and Gridworld setups, demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed robust policy gradient, yielding remarkable improvements in performance compared to existing baselines.

We investigate a novel type of paradox involving probabilistic teams making decisions under uncertainty, specifically a variant involving expected payoffs in a choice-less box game. Our analysis reveals that under certain conditions, nearly all teams encounter an unresolvable situation due to the absence of determinism, even when relying on minimal information or making decisions independently. This occurs in a setting devoid of communication among team members, thereby illustrating the emergence of a paradox without the need for cooperative strategies. Our research demonstrates that the described situation represents a fundamental limitation in scenarios involving uncertainty and probabilistic independence.

Our calculations demonstrate that cubanite, a mineral with the same chemical composition as the simulated structure, exhibits orbital selectivity in the presence of strong correlations without a Mott or hemi-Mott insulating state.  We find that in cubanite, strong hybridization between 3d and 3p states of iron and sulfur respectively causes the splitting of Fe-3d and S-3p states into distinct sub-bands, resulting in overlapping sub-bands that give rise to conductive behavior.  Our analyses using various methodologies, including coherent-incoherent decomposition, show orbital selectivity across various broadening scenarios, and we utilize cubanite as a theoretical model to investigate the nuances of orbital-selective states through its nearly idealized symmetry.  Furthermore, our calculations reveal that marginally separated upper and lower bands produce anomalous physical properties, including unconventional semi-metallic behavior, due to distinct hole pockets at the Fermi level created by the upper band and electron-filled valleys located deep within the Brillouin zone filled by the lower band.

In this research, we observe external magnetic field-independent Rabi oscillations in the giant form, which are caused by random shifts in the location of single electrons residing in quantum dots. Our experiments demonstrate a Rabi period of approximately 2.5 picoseconds and position fluctuations of around 20 Angstroms. These significant Rabi fluctuations in the absence of an external magnetic field offer the potential for external control over electron spin superposition states without relying on external factors.

In two-dimensional non-symmorphic wallpaper group lattices, Dirac points can arise due to path connectivity, with multiple non-symmorphic wall networks exhibiting these points.  Our study provides a comprehensive theoretical framework using a tight-binding model to analyze the electronic properties of these structures.  By adjusting geometric parameters of the non-symmorphic walls within a two-dimensional superlattice, we can modify and even eliminate Dirac points of charge neutrality in various non-symmorphic wall networks.  Specifically, we observe that adding vertical connections to horizontal parallel wires within an oblique wall network results in the opening of a gap at the Dirac point.  Similarly, we use a model Hamiltonian to explain the mechanism of this phenomenon.  Furthermore, our non-symmorphic wall network model demonstrates that light can be controlled and manipulated by changing geometric parameters of the lattice.  With a suitable lattice design, we are able to achieve complete light localization.  These findings provide a framework for light confinement within non-symmorphic wall networks, with potential applications in photonic and photonics systems.

Quantum superposition states, like the coherent states, are sensitive to phase and can be expanded upon with complex amplitudes. However, quantum optics techniques fall short in generating non-Gaussian superpositions of coherent states due to the limited gate set available. We suggest using single-photon quantum-optical transformations, which are straightforward to implement with beam splitters, in conjunction with laser excitation. We demonstrate that this combination enables not only a conversion of photon detection into photon subtraction but also provide a distinct model for interaction with an ancillary single-photon field. Notably, this combination allows for direct manipulation of the phase of quantum states within the single-photon subspace, thus extending the capability of current quantum optics techniques. We also explore the effect of phase on various observables and discuss the potential utility of this technique in quantum optics.

In this work, we employ the Newman-Penrose formalism to delve into the properties of bivectors within classical gravity and general relativity, using the Newman-Penrose scalar notation. The Newman-Penrose formalism is a coordinate-based representation of general relativity that aligns with the Newman-Penrose spinor formalism, which has been shown to be the fundamental framework for understanding gravity and the origin of mass in the Standard Model through the work of Roger Penrose and his colleagues. Before the Newman-Penrose spinor formalism, we examined the role of electromagnetic field bundles in ordinary general relativity within the Newman-Penrose formalism, revealing how diagonalizing the electromagnetic stress-energy tensor leads to non-diagonalized Weyl curvature tensor in the standard four-dimensional Newman-Penrose formalism, as indicated by a detailed mathematical proof. Furthermore, we explored the scenario of an expanding universe with electromagnetic fields and no matter or spin, as modeled by Newman-Penrose constants, which arise naturally from the Newman-Penrose formalism and have deep implications for the quantum gravity regime, including the emergence of Newman-Penrose spinors and the DeWitt-Sweet Hamilton-Jacobi equation in quantum gravity.

The creation of customized polymers is crucial for advancing the field of biomedicine, biotechnology, and material science. Understanding how small molecules interact with surfaces modified with tailored polymers is essential in this domain. Due to the complexity of these systems, obtaining accurate experimental data can be both costly and time-consuming. As a result, the need to efficiently design experiments based on predicted outcomes has become apparent. This study presents a novel polymer design approach, utilizing machine learning to analyze data from small molecule recognition experiments and identify an optimal combination of monomers that maximizes unique molecule recognition. When applied to actual experimental data, this strategy successfully produced a polymer identified by a distinct molecule recognition pattern, validating its potential to reduce the number of required tests while facilitating discovery of novel polymers.

This paper provides an in-depth explanation of a direct transcription methodology for creating optimized schedules, specifically focusing on a dual-patient ventilation scenario as a case study. We begin with a concise overview of direct transcription, then proceed to outline the development of a optimal time-based treatment plan for intubated COVID-19 patients undergoing positive pressure ventilation. Research has shown that employing a direct transcription methodology results in solutions with minimal objective values within five percent of the original problem's threshold. This almost matches the potential benefit suggested by constantly supplied oxygen's potential peak effectiveness. Furthermore, we establish that certain parameters of the optimal solution met a stability criterion, indicating slight modifications to problem details yield optimal solutions with comparable performance characteristics.

Identifying tumors within clinical CT scans is a highly intricate and vital task in medical computer vision. Due to limited annotated data and varying image quality from different hospitals, further enhancement of segmentation models is urgently needed. In this study, we introduce a novel deep learning architecture called DDAUnet, which incorporates spatial attention mechanisms and dilated dense connections to improve segmentation accuracy. Experimental evaluations using public CT datasets demonstrate that our model outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with the DDAUnet achieving a Dice SimilarityCoefficient (DSC) of 0.939, outshining the previous best result (0.887) on the publicly available dataset.

This study is an investigation into well log analysis and uncertainty quantification using an ensemble approach, with specific application to geosteering. We develop a method for estimating measurement uncertainty that accounts for both random and systematic uncertainties, which is particularly useful for well log data. Our findings demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through two examples, including an interval-based linear inversion for resistivity logs and a handling of density logs affected by fluid type variations. One case study illustrates how these methods can be used to manage uncertainty during the drilling process to meet safety criteria, ensuring the avoidance of oil gases inhalation. Our research provides a framework for real-time well log interpretation and risk assessment, ensuring steeper well trajectories can be drilled with confidence.

Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and serves as a starting point for subsequent analysis. NER has also been applied to near-state-of-the-art solutions for extracting summaries from news articles. This work proposes a new approach to nested NER, framing it as parsing entities with complex hierarchical structures. We believe this perspective unifies and clarifies existing methods, providing a foundation for innovating on solutions to nested NER through the use of advanced parsing techniques. Leveraging recent advancements in transformer-based parsers, our proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art results on two benchmarks for nested NER, outperforming previous methodologies and demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach.

We examine the connection between the number of tangible bitangents to a plane quartic and its tropical counterpart, addressing the open query of rationality for this mapping. We establish the correspondence between counted tangible and tropical bitangents as a polynomial in specific invariants of the underlying tropical quartic. This formulation of the relationship enables the derivation of the counting formula for tangible bitangents in terms of tropical data. Additionally, we provide an interpretation for this count through A1-topology.

Research into GPS-free positioning techniques for GPS-denied regions is highly relevant for locating unmonitored threats and enhancing security in highly vulnerable areas. Traditional methods rely on triangulation based on signals from three or more reference nodes, but these methods introduce errors due to packet transmission delays and virtual range offsets caused by different transmission speeds of radio technologies. This paper focuses on reducing such errors in GPS-denied environments by using a hybrid approach that combines 802.15.4 and 802.11 protocols for data transmission. Our research shows an increased localization accuracy of nearly 40% compared to using a single protocol, achieving an average error rate of 3.2 cm out of 1.22 meters, as demonstrated in our experiments within an indoor environment with a highly reflective surface. Furthermore, our results indicate that despite employing two protocols, interference due to simultaneous transmission of different signal types remains manageable, with results showing up to 25% better accuracy than a single protocol, notably without doubling the time required for signal transmission.

This paper offers an in-depth examination of multilingual text generation and
assessment methods, specifically targeting content creation for English-Arabic
and English-Hindi mixed-language communities. It also explores the key issues
that arise in multilingual natural language processing tasks and highlights
critical aspects that influence the development of these technologies in
multilingual societies. The discussion provides valuable insights for future
researchers working on NLP projects in multilingual contexts.
